title: Recognising dental problems in rabbits
subtitle: Rabbit teeth grow continuously. When they stop wearing correctly, the animal stops eating.
excerpt: A rabbit's six incisors and 22 cheek teeth grow roughly 2-3 mm a week. They stay the correct length through constant wear against each other. When alignment fails, through genetics, injury, or low-roughage diet, the resulting spurs, hooks, and elongated roots cause pain that shows first as a change in eating behaviour.
sourceNotes: British Rabbit Council dental health guidance. RWAF (Rabbit Welfare Association and Fund) dental disease factsheet. Frances Harcourt-Brown, Textbook of Rabbit Medicine (2002), dental chapter (specialist reference). RSPCA rabbit dental care notes.

glossaryTerms.definition: Misalignment of the teeth so they do not meet and wear correctly. In rabbits it may be hereditary (especially in lop and dwarf breeds with shortened skulls) or acquired through injury or low hay intake.
Sharp points that develop on cheek teeth when the upper and lower teeth do not wear flat against each other. Spurs cut the tongue and cheek mucosa during chewing.
A slowdown or complete stop of normal gut movement in a rabbit. Dental pain often triggers stasis because the rabbit stops eating hay, which reduces gut motility.

content.text: Rabbit dental disease is the most common reason rabbits stop eating. By the time a rabbit is sitting over its food bowl without eating, the teeth may already have been causing pain for days. Catching the earlier signs prevents the secondary cascade: no eating → no hay intake →
gut stasis
→ emergency vet visit.
Early warning signs
Dropping food, taking pellets into the mouth, then letting them fall.
Eating soft food (pellets) but ignoring hay. Hay requires the grinding motion most affected by cheek tooth spurs.
Weight loss over several weeks with no other obvious cause.
Wet dewlap or chin, saliva builds up when chewing is painful.
Visible incisor
malocclusion
, the four front incisors curve outward rather than meeting in a neat scissor bite.
What you can check yourself

The incisors are visible by gently parting the lips. They should meet so the lower incisors sit just behind and below the upper ones, with a short secondary pair of peg teeth immediately behind the upper incisors. Overgrown incisors that have curved or crossed indicate a vet check is needed.
The cheek teeth (molars and premolars) are not visible without equipment.
Dental spurs

on cheek teeth require a vet exam with an otoscope or direct examination under sedation. If a rabbit is dropping food but the incisors look normal, assume cheek tooth involvement until proven otherwise.
When to go to the vet
Any rabbit not eating for more than 12 hours needs a vet call, not a wait-and-see. Gut stasis develops fast.
Suspected dental spurs are addressed by rasping or burring under sedation. This is not a DIY procedure.

Incisor malocclusion that cannot be corrected may be managed by regular trimming or extraction. Extraction sounds extreme but often improves quality of life. A rabbit without front teeth grinds hay with the cheek teeth and eats well.
Prevention through diet

The single most effective preventative is unlimited hay. The long lateral grinding motion required to break down hay fibres is what wears the cheek teeth flat and prevents spur formation. Pellets require relatively little lateral movement. A rabbit eating 80% hay and 20% pellets by weight has far less dental disease than one on the reverse ratio.
Willow sticks, apple branches, and other gnawable wood enrichment give the incisors work to do but do not address cheek tooth wear. Hay is the only thing that does.
